By Mike Allen · Nov 17, 2026

Good Tuesday afternoon. Today's newsletter, edited by Alex Fitzpatrick, is 778 words, a 3-min. read. Thanks to Kathie Bozanich for copy editing.

👀 Breaking: With America on edge about online outages, the classified internal communications network of the National Security Agency — of all places — went offline today. A statement from the agency blamed the outage on "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance."

  • ✈️ The FAA paused new installations of the Juniper routers linked to last week's ground stop. Get the latest.
 
 
1 big thing: Huang pitches a comeback
 
Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he'd be "honored" to return to the company he co-founded, Axios' Herb Scribner reports.

  • Huang, a towering figure in today's AI boom, left the hugely influential company on Nov. 12 amid reports of multiple affairs, including one with a woman whom the U.S. believes to be a Chinese spy.
  • The fallout has sent tech stocks reeling and raised big questions about Nvidia's business practices, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's handling of the company, and the state of the AI industry.

🤳 Huang wrote on X: "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO."

  • "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

Some Nvidia employees and investors, AI boosters, and even President Trump have called for Huang's return.

  • Trump said yesterday before leaving for his Asia trip: "I would not mind that."
  • "I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another."

✅ Reality check: Nvidia's board has shown zero interest in bringing Huang back.

  • He and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are set to testify before Congress early next month, lawmakers announced today.
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

What's next: Nvidia's post-Huang era begins in earnest with the release of its third-quarter results after trading ends today, Axios' Matt Phillips writes.

  • Investors and analysts will read tea leaves and listen for hints about near-term changes the company is making (or expects the government to make) in response to Huang's resignation and the circumstances surrounding it.

Go deeper.
 
 
2. 🛰️ Voyager's new record
 
Rendering: NASA/JPL-Caltech

At exactly 5:16:07 ET tomorrow morning, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft will become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth, Alex Fitzpatrick writes.

  • At that distance — about 16 billion miles — it takes a full day for light (and thus radio transmissions and operator commands) to travel between Voyager and Earth.

🚀 Launched in 1977, humanity's most distant probe is still transmitting valuable data as it cruises along in interstellar space at nearly 38,000 mph.

  • That's thanks to NASA's Voyager team, which keeps finding novel ways to keep the spacecraft operational.

3. ⚡️ Catch me up
 
President Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul with a signed trade deal today in Manila, Philippines. Photo: Carlos Barria/Reuters
  1. 🇵🇭 President Trump arrived in the Philippines, where he met with regional partners, sought to formalize a trade deal, and got a break from a series of setbacks at home — including major flight disruptions. Trump will fly to China tomorrow for historic nuclear talks on Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Go deeper.
  2. 🦠 The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, as the highly contagious virus has spread at the highest rate in more than 30 years — largely among unvaccinated people. Go deeper.
  3. 🏛️ House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) plans to force his members to take a tallied vote this week on whether to nominate him as Speaker of the House. The plan marks a shift in tactics that would help reveal whether he has the votes to become Speaker on Jan. 3. More from Axios' Andrew Solender.
 
 
4. 🖼️ 1 for the road: NatGeo pics of the year
 
Cover: Tony Wu/National Geographic

National Geographic's Pictures of the Year 2026, out today, features 25 "extraordinary photographs revealing the moments, discoveries, and untold stories that defined the past year."

  • The iconic yellow-bordered mag says: "Selected from more than one million images captured by National Geographic photographers around the globe, this year's collection offers a striking look at the natural world, human ingenuity and the remarkable ways people and wildlife navigate a changing planet."

Above: "How, exactly, eels reproduce is a mystery that has long confounded biologists, and no human on record had ever photographed the act in the wild until Tony Wu did" in Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan, National Geographic says.

  • The cover photo shows a "pair of Abbott's moray eels (Gymnothorax eurostus) reaching the pinnacle of their spawning run, three tenths of a second after leaving the cover of coral. The male on the left is just releasing the jaw of [the] female."
Photo: Jasper Doest/National Geographic

📸 Above, Lorena Masei playfully offers her hat to a horse at the Masei family farm in the Italian Alps.
